The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound for Cuba, as the ⁠Trump administration’s crippling ⁠oil embargo against ​the island nation continued.

The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in the Caribbean Sea between Cuba ⁠and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship ⁠was 91 metres (300ft) long.

item.title: Suicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attack
item.description:
Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation

At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.

Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.

item.title: ‘They want to displace us’: Israel launches new demolition of West Bank olive groves
item.description:
‘They want to displace us’: Israel launches new demolition of West Bank olive groves

Submitted by Mohammed Turkman on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 12:21
Military orders and bulldozers target Palestinian farmland, threatening livelihoods ahead of the olive harvest
A Palestinian walks among olive trees uprooted by Israeli forces on his land in Beit Rima, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank (Mohammed Turkman/MEE)
Off

Standing in his backyard, Saleh Tamimi looked in agony at the remains of olive trees he had tended for years.

Around his home in Deir Nizam, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, the uprooted trees lay in a tangled heap of branches, stones and soil.

Days earlier, Israeli bulldozers had arrived to raze land his family has owned since the 1960s.

“What has this lemon tree done to them and their security?” Tamimi asked Middle East Eye, pointing to the broken branches. 

“I used to water this olive tree every day,” he added, pointing to another.

He said his house has also been issued a demolition order.

“They want to displace us. I have nowhere else to go. Even if they destroy this house, I’m not leaving.”

Tamimi’s case is part of a wider campaign targeting Palestinian agricultural land and olive groves across the occupied West Bank.

In September, a series of military orders demanded the removal of vegetation and uprooting of trees across hundreds of dunams, just weeks before the olive harvest began.

According to data from the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, 55 military orders targeting trees and vegetation were issued between the start of the year and September.

They affected about 2,373 dunams, compared with 47 orders covering 1,613 dunams throughout the whole of 2025.

On 20 September, following the killing of a settler in a shooting near Deir Nizam, the commission said a military order was issued targeting about 99.79 dunams of village land. The order required vegetation to be removed and olive and other trees to be uprooted.

Four days later, another order targeted a further 94.79 dunams, giving landowners 12 hours to remove the trees themselves, according to the commission.

Nathir Tamimi, another landowner in Deir Nizam, said his family owns about 24 dunams planted with olive trees. The trees, he said, had been inherited from previous generations. In recent days, Israeli forces had bulldozed about eight dunams of his land, along with neighbouring plots.

He said about 140 dunams in the area had been cleared so far.

Harvest under threat

The escalation in tree-uprooting orders has affected more than Deir Nizam.

On 24 September, Israeli forces bulldozed about 31 dunams of private land in Beit Rima, northwest of Ramallah, uprooting more than 400 olive trees.

The operation came two days after a military order was issued requiring the removal of the trees. 

'We refused to uproot trees we had planted with our own hands'

– Afrah Sanaf, Beit Rima resident

Hazem Rimawi, 61, said the trees uprooted from his three-dunam plot were heavy with fruit. 

“What happened in a few hours wiped out decades of work,” he told MEE.

“I have no other source of livelihood besides this land and these olive trees. What use is the land now that the trees have been uprooted?”

Afrah Sanaf, another resident affected by the bulldozing, said residents were informed on 22 September of a decision to remove trees in the area.

They went to the municipality to examine the map, only to discover that their land was included in the order.

Sanaf said his land was home to about 138 olive trees, many of them generations old and familiar to his family since childhood.

He said he was 63 and could not remember a time when the trees did not exist.

The notice they received gave landowners 12 hours to remove the trees themselves.

“Naturally, we refused to uproot trees we had planted with our own hands,” he said.

According to Sanaf, the bulldozed land lies about three or four kilometres from the nearest Israeli settlement.

‘Rooted in this land’

On 25 September, Israeli bulldozers began uprooting olive and forest trees in Beit Ur al-Fuqa, southwest of Ramallah.

The operation followed a notice targeting 29 dunams of Palestinian land planted with trees. The order was issued two days after a Palestinian carried out a car-ramming attack at an Israeli checkpoint near the village, injuring an Israeli soldier.

Ali Samara, head of the village council, said the bulldozing had extended to about 60 dunams.

He warned that continued operations could uproot at least 1,500 olive trees, some of them more than 200 years old.

'We are just like the olive trees we inherited: rooted in this land'

– Nathir Tamimi, Deir Nizam resident 

In Kafr Malik, northeast of Ramallah, Israeli authorities issued a military order targeting more than 56 dunams, also calling for the removal of vegetation and olive trees.

The escalation has come as farmers prepare for the olive harvest, which typically begins in October.

For those whose fruit-bearing trees have been uprooted, the loss goes beyond this year’s harvest. The trees themselves can take years to become productive again.

“What happened left us in a state of shock. It was an act of injustice,” said Sanaf.

“The trees and land we lost were the source of livelihood we had relied on all our lives.”

The destruction of terraces and topsoil, along with restrictions on access to farmland, threatens the land’s ability to be cultivated in the future.

“The damage is not limited to the owners of the bulldozed land; it affects the entire town,” said Nathir.

“The landscape has shifted from green olive groves to expanses stripped of their trees.”

Nathir said he believed the uprooting was aimed at pushing landowners off their land. But he added that they remained determined to stay.

“We are just like the olive trees we inherited: rooted in this land.”

Occupation
Fayha Shalash
Ramallah, occupied Palestine

item.title: Morning recap
item.description:
Morning recap

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

If you're just joining us, here are key developments: 

* US President Donald Trump has again said that the war with Iran could end soon, "probably right after the elections", while questioning who in Tehran Washington could negotiate with.

* Trump's top cabinet members met secretly at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, Axios reported, citing three US officials familiar with the matter.

* Yemen’s armed forces say they carried out 71 attacks targeting Houthi gatherings, reinforcements and military buildups across several areas of Taiz province, Al Jazeera reported.

* The death toll from an Israeli strike on an apartment in Gaza City has risen to five, Palestinian medical sources have told Al Jazeera.

* The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a "terrorist" attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.

* Israeli settlers killed 19-year-old Palestinian Bahaa Sami Amin Nathsheh in Kobar, north of the occupied West Bank city of Ramallah, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing the health ministry.

* Debris from a ballistic missile that was shot down in Saudi Arabia's Ahad Rafidah Governorate in the Asir region injured a resident, according to the Saudi Directorate of Civil Defence.

* Two Iranian nationals were charged in Britain with preparing a terrorist attack against the Jewish community in northern England, police said on Friday.

* The master of a crude oil tanker has reported being struck by an unknown projectile 4 nautical miles east of Oman, ⁠according to the United Kingdom ​Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

* Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed, SkyNews reported.

* A source close to the UAE government has accused the Israeli government of exploiting the flydubai incident for political purposes and delaying the restoration of flydubai service, according to Ynet.

* The United States has issued sanctions against three individuals and two France-based charities that it said were part of a network that raised more than $2 million for Hamas, and announced six arrests.

item.title: Trump's top cabinet members discuss Iran, Houthi conflict at Camp David, report says
item.description:
Trump's top cabinet members discuss Iran, Houthi conflict at Camp David, report says

US President Donald Trump's top cabinet members met secretly at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, Axios reported, citing three US officials familiar with the matter.

Axios said the meeting, chaired by Vice President JD Vance, was not announced by the Trump administration, and the last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran.

Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine, the outlet reported.

"Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East.

item.title: Yemeni forces claim 71 attacks on Houthi targets in Taiz
item.description:
Yemeni forces claim 71 attacks on Houthi targets in Taiz

Yemen’s armed forces say they carried out 71 attacks targeting Houthi gatherings, reinforcements and military buildups across several areas of Taiz province, Al Jazeera reported.

A Houthi military spokesperson said the operations targeting al-Aqrud, Samea, al-Ahkum, al-Akboush, Jabal Rasin, Jabal Jardad, Bani Omar, Bani Bakari, al-Kaawish and al-Athawir destroyed several Houthi transport and support vehicles and caused casualties among the group’s fighters.
